rehearse what to say before any interaction
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
The world is a dangerous place

Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

issues.explanation: The cognitive formulation isolates Threat completely, so absence of Threat items is not itself a problem; however, the current profile strongly emphasizes trauma-memory reexperiencing and appraisals without any explicit threat content, making the night-specific avoidance item look weakly anchored to the rest of the selected profile.

issues.item: Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Night' implies fear linked to darkness/outdoor danger, but there are no Threat items and no memory/trigger content tied to night-time, darkness, or outdoor contexts. For this relief-worker trauma, that strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the least coherent item because it addresses a threat context not otherwise represented across Triggers, Memory, or Negative Appraisals.

issues.item: Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
issues.explanation: The formulation isolates Threat completely: all edges to and from Threat are inactive. Yet the selected Threat items are central, high-intensity PTSD threat responses and are also mirrored elsewhere. This makes Threat functionally active in a way that contradicts the formulation structure.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: Threat: Flashbacks and Threat: Physical Reactivity are tightly linked to the Memory and Triggers nodes, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Threat. Including these as Threat items makes the profile inconsistent with the stated node architecture.

issues.item: Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
issues.explanation: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance and Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings both imply an ongoing current-danger/threat monitoring pattern, which again makes Threat clinically central despite Threat being fully disconnected in the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options is the least coherent trigger relative to the rest of the profile. The remaining items focus on moral reminders and nightmare residue, while appraisals and strategies emphasize vigilance, rage, and fear of losing control. Entrapment could occur, but here it lacks a clear connection to the rest of the selected content and weakens coherence.

The cognitive formulation isolates Threat completely: all edges to and from Threat are inactive. However, the selected Threat items describe a prominent, connected threat response cluster (flashbacks, strong physical reactivity, concentration problems from reminders), which is difficult to reconcile with a formulation in which Threat has no active links to Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies.

Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance functions more like a current threat/safety-state belief and implies an active Threat system. That sits poorly with the formulation's fully inactive Threat node, especially when paired with checking surroundings and reactivity/flashback-type threat items.

The Threat node is clinically misaligned with the formulation: all incoming and outgoing Threat edges are inactive, so Threat should be relatively isolated or not central. However, the selected threat items describe an active symptomatic threat response cluster (strong emotional/physical reactivity and concentration disruption) that appears tightly tied to triggers and memory intrusions. This creates a contradiction with the formulation structure, especially given concurrent trigger and memory items that imply exactly the kind of reminder-linked threat activation the model marks as inactive. The other nodes are broadly coherent with each other and with the trauma type.

The Threat node is clinically incoherent with the provided cognitive formulation. Threat has no active incoming or outgoing edges, so it should not appear as a tightly integrated maintaining component. Yet all three selected Threat items are non-specific PTSD symptom/severity indicators rather than a coherent sense of current threat, and they are not meaningfully linked to the active Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies pattern.

Threat is structurally isolated in the formulation, but 'Scanning for Danger' is tightly mirrored by both Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings' and Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time,' making threat function as an active linked node rather than an isolated one.

Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time' overlaps almost exactly with Threat: 'Scanning for Danger' and Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings,' which contradicts the formulation because Threat has no active links to or from these nodes.

Threat: 'Negative Emotions' is very broad and non-specific, while the rest of the profile centers on intrusive reliving, moral/entrapment triggers, and vigilance-based coping; as a Threat item it does not fit the otherwise isolated, weakly integrated role of threat in this formulation.

vignette:
Thanh is an eighty-year-old widowed Vietnamese-American man who spent much of his career as a data scientist but who, in his mid-sixties, volunteered for two extended deployments as a relief worker in an active conflict zone in Southeast Asia. What he witnessed there - malnourished children being turned away from supply convoys by armed factions, colleagues shot at checkpoints, the bureaucratic paralysis that left entire villages without aid while he stood helpless with clipboards and satellite phones - left marks that did not surface fully until years later. The specific texture of those moments matters: the feeling of having no options, of watching moral order collapse in front of him while institutional constraints made intervention impossible, became the emotional signature of the trauma. He returned home, cared for his ailing wife until her death three years ago, and managed, for a time, to hold the memories at a distance. It was only after her death removed his last stabilising relationship that the symptoms began to consolidate into something he could no longer manage alone.

Thanh now lives by himself in a quiet suburb of Seattle, working part-time as a remote data scientist - a role that, ironically, keeps him tethered to screens and news feeds for much of the day. It is in that occupational context that one of his most reliable triggers appears: news reports about humanitarian crises, armed conflict, or supply-chain failures will surface in aggregated feeds while he works, and when they do, the memories do not arrive as recollections but as immediate experience. He has come to dread the moment a headline loads before he can look away, because he is certain that what follows will not feel like reading about something distant - it will feel like being back at the checkpoint, paralysed, watching something terrible unfold. The memory arrives with the quality of film on a loop: the same sequence of images, the same sounds, the same visceral sense that it is happening now rather than fifteen years ago. Waking from nightmares - which come several times a week - produces the same collapse of temporal distance, so that mornings carry the residue of the night into the first hours of his working day.

Because the memories feel so present and so uncontrollable, Thanh has come to believe that his mind is failing him in a fundamental way - that the intensity and repetition of what he experiences means he is losing his grip on reality. He is also frightened of his own anger. In the conflict zone he had witnessed what unchecked rage could do, and he is convinced that the irritability he now feels constantly - the short fuse that ignites during video calls, the aggressive edge that enters his voice when colleagues make careless remarks - means he is capable of something terrible. These appraisals, the fear of going crazy and the fear of his own rage, feed directly back into hypervigilance: if he believes the world is dangerous and that he himself is a potential source of harm, then every interaction must be monitored and prepared for. He rehearses conversations before any meeting, scripting his responses to avoid the moment where anger might break through. He scans his environment constantly, reading the body language of delivery drivers and neighbours the way he once read the demeanour of armed guards. These strategies, intended to contain the threat, instead keep his nervous system perpetually primed, and a body that never fully relaxes is a body that finds danger everywhere - which means ordinary moments of mild social friction or moral transgression, someone cutting in line, a colleague dismissing a concern, register as genuine violations and pull the checkpoint back into the present.

The loop tightens in a particular way: the rehearsal and the scanning prevent him from ever having an experience that disconfirms the threat, so the appraisals calcify, and the memories remain unprocessed and easily activated. He avoids news deliberately, but the avoidance means he never learns that he can tolerate exposure without disintegrating, and so the triggers retain their full potency.

What finally brought Thanh to seek help was a video call last month in which he lost his temper with a junior colleague over a minor data error. He did not shout, but the cold fury in his voice frightened him. He is eighty years old, he is alone, and what he is most afraid of is that he has become, in some irreversible way, a dangerous man. What he is most hoping for is that someone can tell him otherwise.
